methodological_rigor.justification: Large retrospective cohort (n=650) with rigorous methodology including multivariable logistic regression, linear mixed-effects models for repeated inflammatory markers, and subgroup analyses. Strong baseline balance across analgesia groups (age, BMI, ASA, comorbidity, tumor stage, surgical approach all p>0.05). Advanced statistical adjustments for confounders. Good model calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.42-0.37). Limitation: retrospective design and single-center setting.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual retrospective cohort with direct clinical endpoints highly relevant to gynecologic oncology practice. Demonstrates clear benefit of multimodal analgesia: shortened LOS (6.5 vs 8.2 days, p<0.001), reduced complications (13% vs 21.8%, p=0.04), attenuated inflammatory response (NLR/CRP p<0.001), improved pain control (NRS 3.2 vs 4.8, p<0.001). Practical implications for perioperative care optimization and alignment with SOAPC guidelines.

reporting_quality.justification: Comprehensive STROBE-aligned reporting with detailed study design, inclusion/exclusion criteria, analgesia group classification, outcome definitions (Clavien-Dindo, NRS, PONV, time to ambulation/flatus), and statistical methods clearly specified. Baseline characteristics table well-balanced. Multivariate models thoroughly documented. However, no explicit data availability statement. Limited post-discharge follow-up (mentioned as limitation).

novelty_literature.justification: Multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia well-established in general surgery; study extends to gynecologic cancer with large disease-specific cohort and systematic comparison of four analgesic strategies. Novel contribution: integration of inflammatory biomarker trajectories (NLR, CRP) with clinical recovery outcomes and subgroup stability analysis. Advances existing knowledge but follows established paradigm rather than introducing new mechanism.

writing_presentation.justification: Excellent organization with clear narrative progression from introduction through discussion of mechanisms and limitations. Methods comprehensively detailed with explicit outcome definitions and statistical approaches. Results systematically presented with appropriate use of tables (baseline characteristics, outcomes, multivariate models, subgroup analyses). Discussion mechanistically grounded with appropriate citation of prior literature and clear statement of study limitations.

key_strengths: Large, well-balanced retrospective cohort (n=650) with systematic stratification into four analgesia groups and minimal missing data (<5%)

Rigorous multivariable adjustment with validated statistical approaches (logistic regression, mixed-effects models) and subgroup stability across age, BMI, surgical approach, FIGO stage, and diabetes status

Comprehensive outcome measurement: clinical endpoints (LOS, complications, time to ambulation/flatus), patient-centered (pain scores, PONV), and mechanistic inflammatory markers (NLR, CRP trajectories)
Clinically actionable findings: multimodal analgesia independently reduced prolonged hospitalization (OR 0.52, p=0.013) and complications (OR 0.55, p=0.048)
Clear alignment with guideline-concordant care (SOAPC recommendations) with potential to improve perioperative and oncologic outcomes
key_concerns: Retrospective observational design with inherent limitation that analgesia group allocation reflects clinical practice rather than randomization—residual confounding possible despite rigorous adjustment
Single tertiary center in Southwest China with established high ERAS adherence (not representative of broader clinical settings with lower perioperative infrastructure)
In-hospital outcome analysis only; post-discharge complications and readmissions not systematically captured, potentially underestimating total morbidity
No long-term follow-up data on oncologic outcomes; immune-inflammatory benefits during hospital stay may not translate to improved cancer-specific survival
Pharmacological details of regional blocks (epidural vs TAP/QLB) pooled—differential efficacy not analyzed
chief_reviewer.rationale: High-quality retrospective cohort demonstrating clinically significant benefits of multimodal analgesia in endometrial cancer surgery with rigorous statistical methods and consistent effects across subgroups. Suitable for tier 2 publication pending prospective multicenter validation and longer-term oncologic outcome assessment.
